claim: T cells use kinetic proofreading to discriminate antigens by converting small changes in antigen-binding lifetime into large differences in cell activation.
source: T cells use kinetic proofreading to discriminate antigens by converting small changes in antigen-binding lifetime into large differences in cell activation, but where in the signaling cascade this computation is performed is unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known concept in the field, supported by the broader literature on T cell signaling.

claim: The location in the signaling cascade where kinetic proofreading computation is performed was previously unknown.
source: T cells use kinetic proofreading to discriminate antigens by converting small changes in antigen-binding lifetime into large differences in cell activation, but where in the signaling cascade this computation is performed is unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: A light-gated immune receptor was previously developed to probe the role of ligand kinetics in T cell antigen signaling.
source: Previously, we developed a light-gated immune receptor to probe the role of ligand kinetics in T cell antigen signaling.
evidence: This refers to prior work by the authors, citing their previous publication (Tischer and Weiner, 2019).

claim: Significant kinetic proofreading was previously found at the level of diacylglycerol (DAG).
source: We found significant kinetic proofreading at the level of the signaling lipid diacylglycerol (DAG) but lacked the ability to determine where the multiple signaling steps required for kinetic discrimination originate in the upstream signaling cascade (Tiseher and Weiner, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, supported by citation.

claim: The previous optogenetic system lacked the ability to determine where multiple upstream proofreading steps originate.
source: We found significant kinetic proofreading at the level of the signaling lipid diacylglycerol (DAG) but lacked the ability to determine where the multiple signaling steps required for kinetic discrimination originate in the upstream signaling cascade (Tiseher and Weiner, 2019).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the previous experimental system.

claim: The optogenetic system was adapted for robust activation of early signaling events.
source: Here, we uncover where kinetic proofreading is executed by adapting our optogenetic system for robust activation of early signaling events.
evidence: This describes the methodological improvement made in the current study.

claim: The strength of kinetic proofreading progressively increases from Zap70 recruitment to LAT clustering to downstream DAG generation.
source: We find the strength of kinetic proofreading progressively increases from Zap70 recruitment to LAT clustering to downstream DAG generation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Downstream signaling events have slower reset rates than upstream events.
source: Leveraging the ability of our system to rapidly disengage ligand binding, we also measure slower reset rates for downstream signaling events.
evidence: This is a finding from the reset rate experiments presented in Figure 5.

claim: The data suggest a distributed kinetic proofreading mechanism with proofreading steps at both the receptor and downstream signaling complexes.
source: These data suggest a distributed kinetic proofreading mechanism, with proofreading steps both at the receptor and at slower resetting downstream signaling complexes that could help balance antigen sensitivity and discrimination.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Failure of T cells to activate in response to foreign antigen can enable pathogens to invade the body undetected.
source: Failure of T cells to activate in response to foreign antigen can enable pathogens to invade the body undetected (Charles A Janeway et al., 2001; Horst et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Improper T cell activation against self-antigen causes autoimmune disorders.
source: Conversely, improper T cell activation against self-antigen causes autoimmune disorders (Dornmair et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature.

claim: T cells can detect the presence of 1–10 molecules of foreign antigen when contacting an antigen-presenting cell.
source: When a T cell contacts an antigen-presenting cell (APC), it can detect the presence of 1–10 molecules of foreign antigen (Christinck et al., 1991; Demotz et al., 1990; Kimachi et al., 1997; Sykulev et al., 1996), despite the much greater abundance (×100,000 or more) of self-antigen (Bhardwaj et al., 1993; Cohen et al., 2003; Irvine et al., 2002; Unternaehrer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Self-antigen is present at 100,000-fold or greater abundance compared to foreign antigen.
source: When a T cell contacts an antigen-presenting cell (APC), it can detect the presence of 1–10 molecules of foreign antigen (Christinck et al., 1991; Demotz et al., 1990; Kimachi et al., 1997; Sykulev et al., 1996), despite the much greater abundance (×100,000 or more) of self-antigen (Bhardwaj et al., 1993; Cohen et al., 2003; Irvine et al., 2002; Unternaehrer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: T cells must use parameters other than the number of ligand-bound receptors to distinguish self from foreign antigen.
source: These observations indicate that T cells must use parameters other than the number of ligand-bound receptors to distinguish self from foreign antigen (Daniels et al., 2006; Davis et al., 1998; Gascoigne et al., 2001; Germain and Stefanová, 1999).
evidence: This is an inference from the observations about antigen abundance, supported by citations.

claim: The kinetic proofreading model postulates that only antigens that continuously bind a TCR for a sufficient duration activate the T cell.
source: One attractive model for how T cells discriminate antigen is the kinetic proofreading model (Hopfield, 1974; McKeithan, 1995; Ninio, 1975), where only antigens that continuously bind a TCR for a sufficient duration activate the T cell (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the kinetic proofreading model with citations to foundational papers.

claim: Kinetic proofreading postulates that antigen binding initiates a series of sequential biochemical events that are substantially slower than antigen-binding lifetimes.
source: Kinetic proofreading postulates that antigen binding initiates a series of sequential biochemical events that are substantially slower than antigen-binding lifetimes and must progress to completion before activating the T cell.
evidence: This is a description of the kinetic proofreading model mechanism.

claim: Only antigen that stays bound to the TCR long enough for completion of all proofreading events is stimulatory to the T cell.
source: Only antigen that stays bound to the TCR long enough for the completion of all events is stimulatory to the T cell (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a key prediction of the kinetic proofreading model, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: If antigen unbinds the TCR before all proofreading events are complete, the system resets back to the ground state.
source: If the antigen unbinds the TCR before all events are complete, the system resets back to the ground state (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a key feature of the kinetic proofreading model, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: It is commonly accepted that T cells use kinetic proofreading for antigen discrimination.
source: While it is commonly accepted that T cells use kinetic proofreading for antigen discrimination (Coombs and Goldstein, 2005; Courtney et al., 2018; McKeithan, 1995), we do not know which steps in the antigen signal transduction cascade enable the strong kinetic proofreading observed in T cell activation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The specific steps in the antigen signal transduction cascade that enable kinetic proofreading were previously unknown.
source: While it is commonly accepted that T cells use kinetic proofreading for antigen discrimination (Coombs and Goldstein, 2005; Courtney et al., 2018; McKeithan, 1995), we do not know which steps in the antigen signal transduction cascade enable the strong kinetic proofreading observed in T cell activation.
evidence: This establishes the knowledge gap addressed by the study.

claim: Kinetic proofreading can convert small differences in ligand-binding lifetime into large differences in cellular output.
source: Kinetic proofreading can convert small differences in ligand-binding lifetime into large differences in cellular output.
evidence: This is a fundamental property of kinetic proofreading systems.

claim: The number of proofreading steps sets the strength of a proofreading system.
source: The number of proofreading steps sets the strength of a proofreading system, with stronger proofreading systems requiring a higher number of proofreading steps.
evidence: This is a theoretical property of kinetic proofreading systems.

claim: Ten steps of kinetic proofreading would roughly amplify a twofold difference in ligand-binding lifetime into a 1000-fold difference in output.
source: Ten steps of kinetic proofreading would roughly amplify a twofold difference in ligand-binding lifetime into a 1000-fold difference in output.
evidence: This is a quantitative prediction based on kinetic proofreading theory.

claim: Kinetic proofreading allows T cells to ignore numerous shorter-lived self-antigen-binding events while activating in response to rare longer-lived foreign antigen-binding events.
source: Kinetic proofreading allows T cells to ignore numerous shorter-lived self-antigen-binding events, while activating in response to rare longer-lived foreign antigen-binding events (Davis et al., 1998; Gascoigne et al., 2001; Germain and Stefanová, 1999).
evidence: This is a functional consequence of kinetic proofreading, supported by citations.

claim: The light-gated immune receptor system uses a supported lipid bilayer functionalized with LOV2 to create an artificial antigen-presenting surface.
source: A supported lipid bilayer (SLB) functionalized with the light-sensitive protein LOV2 creates an artificial antigen-presenting surface.
evidence: This describes the experimental system, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Jurkat cells expressing zdk-CAR bind dark-state LOV2 and activate antigen signaling.
source: Jurkat cells expressing zdk-CAR bind dark-state LOV2 and activate antigen signaling.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the optogenetic system, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Blue light interrupts LOV2-CAR-binding events and terminates signaling.
source: Blue light interrupts LOV2-CAR-binding events and terminates signaling.
evidence: This describes the light-controlled behavior of the system, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The previous adhesion method using biotinylated beta2 microglobulin antibodies limited the spatiotemporal dynamics of many biosensors.
source: In our previous work, we adhered cells to the SLB through biotinylated beta2 microglobulin antibodies against the cells' MHC class1 (left). This adhesion technique limited the spatiotemporal dynamics of many biosensors, including the recruitment of ZAP70 and the clustering of LAT.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the previous method, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ICAM-1 adhesion improved the spatiotemporal dynamics of LOV2 binding, Zap70 recruitment, LAT clustering, and DAG generation biosensors.
source: SLB adhesion through ICAM-1 improved the spatiotemporal dynamics of each biosensor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2E showing improved fold-change for all biosensors.

claim: ICAM-1 adhesion resulted in statistically significant improvements in maximum fold-change for all biosensors compared to antibody adhesion.
source: Boxplot of the maximum fold-change in LOV2 binding, Zap70 recruitment, LAT clustering, and DAG generation between active and inactive Zdk-CAR signaling states under antibody adhesion and ICAM-1 adhesion. Dashed line indicates population mean, each plot represents reporter change of approximately n=120cells, independent t-test p-values shown.
evidence: Figure 2E shows boxplots with p-values indicating statistical significance.

claim: Zap70 recruitment shows moderate kinetic proofreading with n=4.5 ± 0.4 proofreading steps.
source: Our model indicates a moderate degree of proofreading at Zap70 recruitment across three datasets (n=4.5 ± 0.4) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Zap70 recruitment correlated with both receptor occupancy (ρ=0.42) and ligand-binding half-life (ρ=0.49).
source: Zap70 recruitment correlated with both receptor occupancy (⍴=0.42) and ligand-binding half-life (⍴=0.49) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LAT clustering shows stronger kinetic proofreading with n=7.8 ± 1.1 proofreading steps.
source: Our proofreading model fits our LAT clustering data with a higher degree of proofreading (n=7.8 ±1.1) compared to Zap70 recruitment (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from model fitting shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LAT clustering showed increased dependency on binding half-life (ρ=0.54) and decreased dependence on receptor occupancy (ρ=0.21) compared to Zap70 recruitment.
source: LAT clustering showed an increased dependency on binding half-life (⍴=0.54) and a decreased dependence on receptor occupancy (⍴=0.21) compared to Zap70 recruitment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DAG generation shows the highest degree of kinetic proofreading with n=11.3 ± 1.5 proofreading steps.
source: Our model fits the highest degree of kinetic proofreading at DAG generation (n=11.3 ± 1.5), suggesting further kinetic proofreading steps beyond initial LAT clustering and upstream of DAG generation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from model fitting shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DAG generation depended heavily on ligand half-life (ρ=0.52) while depending least on occupancy (ρ=0.18).
source: The generation of DAG also depended heavily on ligand half-life (⍴=0.52), while depending the least on occupancy (⍴=0.18) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The sequential increase in kinetic proofreading strength suggests proofreading steps exist throughout the cascade up to DAG generation.
source: The sequential increase in the degree of kinetic proofreading progressing down the antigen signaling cascade suggests steps contributing to kinetic proofreading exist throughout the cascade, at least up to the generation of DAG (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the progressive increase in n values shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Additional kinetic proofreading steps exist between Zap70 recruitment and LAT cluster formation.
source: The stronger degree of kinetic proofreading at LAT clustering versus Zap70 recruitment suggests additional steps of kinetic proofreading between the recruitment of Zap70 to phosphorylated ITAMs and the formation of LAT clusters.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in n values between Zap70 and LAT.

claim: Kinetic proofreading steps exist between ligand binding and Zap70 recruitment.
source: These data suggest the existence of kinetic proofreading steps between ligand binding and Zap70 recruitment.
evidence: This is inferred from the non-zero n value measured for Zap70 recruitment.

claim: The lifetimes of bound LOV2 fit an exponential distribution with a mean lifetime of 3.3 seconds.
source: We found the lifetimes of bound LOV2 and recruited Zap70 best fit exponential distributions with mean lifetimes of 3.3 and 9.3 s, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from lifetime distribution analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The lifetimes of recruited Zap70 fit an exponential distribution with a mean lifetime of 9.3 seconds.
source: We found the lifetimes of bound LOV2 and recruited Zap70 best fit exponential distributions with mean lifetimes of 3.3 and 9.3 s, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from lifetime distribution analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The lifetimes of LAT clusters fit a two-step Erlang distribution with a mean lifetime of 14.2 seconds.
source: However, the lifetimes of LAT clusters best fit a two-step Erlang distribution (shape = 2) with a mean lifetime of 14.2 s (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from lifetime distribution analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: LAT clusters reset through a slower multistep process compared to Zap70 recruitment.
source: Upon ligand unbinding, recruited Zap70 and clustered LAT likely reset through different processes, with LAT resetting through a slower multistep process.
evidence: This is inferred from the different distribution fits (exponential vs. Erlang) and longer mean lifetime for LAT.

claim: LOV2 unbinding and Zap70 dissociation suggest a one-step reset process.
source: The lifetime distributions of LOV2 unbinding and Zap70 dissociation fit exponential distributions with mean lifetimes of 3.3 and 9.3 s, respectively, suggesting a one-step reset process.
evidence: This is inferred from the exponential distribution fits shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A LAT cluster could survive a momentary ligand unbinding event and integrate multiple ligand-binding events.
source: While this idea awaits experimental verification, these data open the possibility that a LAT cluster could survive a momentary ligand unbinding event (loss of Zap70) and survive long enough to integrate multiple ligand-binding events, as observed in primary T cells on SLBs with native ligand (Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the slower LAT reset rate, with citation to supporting observations.

claim: Ligand binding excludes the bulky phosphatase CD45 that would otherwise rapidly dephosphorylate the ITAMs.
source: Ligand binding excludes the bulky phosphatase CD45 that would otherwise rapidly dephosphorylate the ITAMs (Davis and van der Merwe, 2006; Springer, 1990).
evidence: This is a known mechanism in T cell signaling, supported by citations.

claim: The receptor could undergo mechanical conformational changes making it more accessible for phosphorylation.
source: The receptor itself could undergo mechanical conformational changes making it more accessible for phosphorylation (Kim et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations.

claim: An active molecule of Lck must phosphorylate the receptor.
source: An active molecule of the src-family-kinase Lck must phosphorylate the receptor (Schoenborn et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a known step in T cell signaling, supported by citations.

claim: Zap70 must overcome autoinhibition before binding the phosphorylated receptor with both of its tandem SH2 domains.
source: Finally, Zap70 must overcome autoinhibition before binding the phosphorylated receptor with both of its tandem SH2 domains (Deindl et al., 2009; Hsu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a known mechanism in Zap70 activation, supported by citations.

claim: Hyperactive Zap70 mutants biased toward the active conformation increase T cell response to normally weak agonists.
source: Hyperactive Zap70 mutants biased toward the active conformation increase T cell response to normally weak agonists, suggesting that pre-activation of Zap70 short-circuits one or more proofreading steps (Shen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an observation from the literature that supports the existence of proofreading steps at Zap70.

claim: LAT does not require phosphorylation of all its tyrosine residues or binding of all known associated proteins to cluster.
source: LAT does not require the phosphorylation of all its tyrosine residues, or binding of all known associated proteins, to cluster (Su et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a known property of LAT clustering, supported by citation.

claim: LAT Y132 is an evolutionarily conserved poor substrate for its kinase Zap70.
source: A strong candidate for an additional proofreading step is phosphorylation of LAT Y132. Y132 is an evolutionarily conserved poor substrate for its kinase Zap70, and this phosphorylation site is required for PLCγ recruitment, DAG generation, and Ca++ mobilization (Andreotti et al., 2010; Courtney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a known property of LAT Y132, supported by citations.

claim: Mutation of residues around LAT Y132 to a better Zap70 substrate resulted in decreased T cell antigen discrimination.
source: Mutation of the residues around Y132 to a better Zap70 substrate that is more rapidly phosphorylated resulted in decreased T cell antigen discrimination (i.e. strong activation to weak agonists; Lo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: PLCγ is recruited to only a subset of LAT clusters.
source: Furthermore, Sherman et al., 2011 found that PLCγ is recruited to only a subset of LAT clusters, suggesting that only a subset of LAT clusters reach a fully signaling-competent state.
evidence: This is an observation from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: TCR/Zap70 and LAT/PLCγ microclusters form spatially segregated domains that remain adjacent to one another.
source: While TCR/Zap70 and LAT/PLCγ microclusters form spatially segregated domains, these domains remain adjacent to one another (Yi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an observation from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: The protein Lck binds Zap70 with its SH2 domain and LAT with its SH3 domain, potentially bridging the two signaling domains.
source: Lo et al., 2018, demonstrated that the protein Lck binds Zap70 with its SH2 domain and LAT with its SH3 domain, potentially bridging the two signaling domains together and propagating binding information.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy measured TCR/CD45 segregated regions within seconds of antigen contact at the tips of T cell microvilli.
source: Super-resolution microscopy by Razvag et al., 2018 measured TCR/CD45 segregated regions within seconds of antigen contact at the tips of T cell microvilli.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: LAT clusters exclude CD45 in reconstituted bilayer systems, potentially limiting dephosphorylation to LAT molecules at the edges of the cluster.
source: LAT clusters exclude CD45 in reconstituted bilayer systems, potentially limiting the dephosphorylation to LAT molecules at the edges of the cluster thus slowing reset (Su et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an observation from the literature with an inferred consequence, supported by citation.

claim: Larger TCR cluster size increases the probability of T cell activation.
source: Consistent with this idea, larger TCR cluster size increases the probability of T cell activation (Manz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an observation from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Shorter binding events that overlapped in space and time activated NFAT translocation similar to long-lived single binding events in primary murine T cells.
source: Lin et al., 2019, also observed cooperativity between single TCR/pMHC-binding events, where shorter binding events that overlapped in space and time activated NFAT translocation similar to long-lived single binding events in primary murine T cells.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Timothy McKeithan postulated that a kinetic proofreading system with slower reset rates for downstream events would respond to cognate-antigen more frequently while still ignoring weak self-antigen.
source: Work on kinetic proofreading often assumes that the reset rate after ligand binding is uniform across all signaling intermediates (koff, Figure 1A). However, in his seminal work applying the mathematical framework of kinetic proofreading to TCR activation, Timothy McKeithan postulated that a kinetic proofreading system with slower reset rates for downstream events compared to upstream signaling events would respond to true cognate-antigen-binding events a higher percentage of the time while still ignoring weak self-antigen-binding events (McKeithan, 1995).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Harris et al. quantified the reset rate of Ca++ release to be 29 seconds and ERK phosphorylation to be 3 minutes upon signal inhibition.
source: Recently, Harris et al. quantified the reset rate of the downstream signaling events Ca++ release and ERK phosphorylation upon signal inhibition to be 29 s and 3 min, respectively (Harris et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Both Ca++ and ERK levels can persist across short inhibitions of signaling.
source: They showed both Ca++ and ERK levels can persist across short inhibitions of signaling.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Harris et al., 2021.

claim: The dissolution of LAT clusters is directly triggered by the unbinding of ligand from the TCR.
source: The dissolution of LAT clusters is directly triggered by the unbinding of ligand from the TCR, and both the TCR and LAT are de-phosphorylated by CD45.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations in this study.

claim: The rate of ERK dephosphorylation or cytosolic Ca++ depletion is not accelerated by TCR unbinding.
source: To our knowledge, the rate of ERK dephosphorylation or cytosolic Ca++ depletion is not accelerated by TCR unbinding, and is turned over through constant rather than agonist-gated degradation.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge in the field.

claim: Cooperativity between active receptors could explain T cell activation in response to intermediate affinity self- and tumor antigens.
source: Cooperativity between active receptors to complete downstream proofreading steps could explain observations of T cell activation in response to intermediate affinity self- and tumor antigens (Yin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observations in the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Cooperativity mechanisms have been implicated in autoimmunity.
source: Such a cooperativity mechanism has been implicated in autoimmunity (Korem Kohanim et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020) and immunotherapy off-target effects (Cameron et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Cooperativity mechanisms have been implicated in immunotherapy off-target effects.
source: Such a cooperativity mechanism has been implicated in autoimmunity (Korem Kohanim et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020) and immunotherapy off-target effects (Cameron et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Jurkats on ICAM-1 functionalized bilayers released a greater percentage of bound LOV2 ligand upon blue-light illumination compared to antibody-based adhesion.
source: Compared to our previous antibody-based adhesion, Jurkats on ICAM-1 functionalized bilayers released a greater percentage of the bound LOV2 ligand upon blue-light illumination.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the two adhesion methods.

claim: ICAM-1 adhered cells displayed receptor/Zap70 and LAT clustering spatial patterns similar to those observed with native receptor ligands on SLBs.
source: ICAM-1 adhered cells also displayed receptor/Zap70 and LAT clustering spatial patterns similar to those observed by others using native receptor ligands on SLBs (Balagopalan et al., 2015; Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014; Kumari et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from the current study compared to literature, supported by citations.

claim: The lentiviral vectors used result in cell-to-cell variability in expression levels of constructs.
source: The lentiviral vectors we used to express our zdk-CAR and live-cell biosensors result in cell-to-cell variability in the expression level of each construct, even after sorting for cells with CAR expression levels similar to native TCR expression in T cells (Tischer and Weiner, 2019).
evidence: This describes a property of the experimental system.

claim: Native T cells vary in TCR expression level and can respond to antigen even at very low levels of TCR expression.
source: Importantly, the variability in receptor expression is not unique to our CAR system; native T cells also vary in TCR expression level and can respond to antigen even at very low levels of TCR expression (Labrecque et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a known property of native T cells, supported by citation.

claim: Kinetic proofreading systems behave differently than non-proofreading systems at steady state.
source: Kinetic proofreading systems behave differently than non-proofreading systems at steady state.
evidence: This is a theoretical property of kinetic proofreading systems.

claim: A non-proofreading system's steady-state output is set by the number of ligand-bound receptors and not the binding half-lives of those ligands.
source: A non-proofreading system's steady-state output is set by the number of ligand-bound receptors and not the binding half-lives of those ligands (Figure 3D, left; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a theoretical property demonstrated in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A kinetic proofreading system can produce different steady-state outputs in response to ligands of different binding half-lives, even when ligand densities are adjusted to achieve equivalent occupancy.
source: In contrast, a kinetic proofreading system can produce different steady-state outputs in response to ligands of different binding half-lives, even when ligand densities are adjusted to achieve equivalent occupancy (Daniels et al., 2006; Figure 3D, right; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a theoretical property demonstrated in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, with citation support.

claim: Signaling events take varying amounts of time to occur after ligand binding on the order of tens of seconds.
source: Signaling events take varying amounts of time to occur after ligand binding (Lin et al., 2019; Yi et al., 2019). However, the temporal delays between steps are on the order of tens of seconds.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Models with unique N values for all three signaling steps (Zap70, LAT, DAG) have the lowest AIC and best explain the data.
source: Models with unique N values for all three signaling steps have the lowest AIC, thus best explaining our data.
evidence: This is a result from AIC model selection analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Models where LAT and DAG share the same N value have only marginally worse AIC than models with unique N values.
source: However, models where LAT and DAG share the same N value (and Zap70 has a unique N value) have only marginally worse AIC (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a result from AIC model selection analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: An 11-step kinetic proofreading system could achieve an error rate less than 0.001 at moderate half-life ratios and concentration ratios.
source: At moderate half-life ratios, an 11-step network can discriminate cognate peptides present in small concentrations (e.g. 1 cognate-ligand per 1000 self-ligands at a half-life ratio of 6).
evidence: This is a result from modeling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: An 11-step network is insufficient to discriminate between ligands with a half-life ratio of 2, even at equal concentrations of cognate- and self-ligand.
source: However, an 11-step network is insufficient to discriminate between ligands with a half-life ratio of 2, even at the high ligand ratio of 1 (equal concentrations of cognate- and self-ligand).
evidence: This is a result from modeling analysis.

claim: Cells are likely detecting longer-lived binding events from the underlying distribution of half-lives rather than the average ligand-binding half-life.
source: This suggests that our cells are unlikely to be detecting the average ligand-binding half-life of each blue-light condition, but are more likely detecting longer-lived binding events from the underlying distribution of half-lives.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the discrepancy between model predictions and experimental conditions.

claim: In vitro washout measurements may differ from the half-lives of ligand-receptor interactions between the cell's plasma membrane and the supported lipid bilayer.
source: Another possibility is that our in vitro washout measurements, which measure average ligand-binding half-lives of soluble ligands diffusing in three dimensions, differ from the half-lives of ligand-receptor interactions between the cell's plasma membrane and the supported lipid bilayer diffusing in two dimensions (Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the discrepancy, with citation support.

claim: At least 14 steps are needed to discriminate between ligands with a half-life ratio of 2 when ligands are at equal concentrations.
source: To discriminate between ligands with a half-life ratio of 2, at least 14 steps are needed when the ligands are at equal concentrations, and more than 25 steps are needed if cognate-ligands are 1 per 1000 self-ligands.
evidence: This is a result from modeling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The required number of proofreading steps decreases rapidly as the half-life ratio increases.
source: The required number of proofreading steps decreases rapidly as the half-life ratio increases, reaching a minimum of eight steps needed for a concentration ratio of 1 per 1000 and a half-life ratio of 10, which is more in line with physiological half-life ratios between agonist and non-agonist peptides (Davis et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a result from modeling analysis with citation to physiological parameters.

claim: The fit N values may be somewhat inflated due to using average ligand-binding half-lives from three-dimensional washout experiments instead of two-dimensional single-molecule information.
source: After comparing our results with the Ganti model, this analysis suggests that our number of fit proofreading steps may be somewhat inflated as a function of our uses the average ligand-binding half-lives of three-dimensional washout experiments in place of the two-dimensional single-molecule information T cells use to make activation decisions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling analysis results.

claim: The higher fit N values are more consistent with the required number of steps to discriminate ligands under physiological conditions than the previous measurements of approximately three steps.
source: However, the higher fit N values are more consistent with the required number of steps to discriminate ligands under more physiological conditions than our previous measurements of approximately three steps, which would not be expected to discriminate ligands with half-life ratio of 10 even at a ligand ratio of 1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B, right).
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing current and previous results to theoretical predictions.
